## Oct 12 Results: A Complete Whiff

Let me give it to you straight—yesterday was a statistical anomaly in the worst way possible. We went 0-for-2, posting a 0.0% accuracy rate. Both picks missed, including a 63% confidence play on the Rays that didn't materialize. These are the days that remind us why we track long-term performance metrics.

## The Data Breakdown

The Rays pick at 63% confidence was particularly frustrating from a statistical standpoint. That's a scenario where our model identified significant edge, yet variance won out. The Dodgers pick was essentially a coin flip at 50%, so that miss stings less from a pure probability perspective.

What concerns me more: we had zero margin for error and hit neither. Small sample size, yes, but 0-2 days require immediate review of recent input variables.

## Oct 13 Preview: Back to the Rays Well

Here's where it gets interesting from a statistical perspective—tomorrow's top pick has us right back on the Tampa Bay Rays. Same team, new game, 53% confidence level. The matchup features Parker Messick taking the mound for Cleveland against Freddy Peralta for Tampa Bay.

## The Numbers on Tomorrow's Pick

The 53% confidence interval tells you everything you need to know—this is a marginal edge play. Peralta's home splits and Messick's limited track record create a narrow but quantifiable advantage for Tampa Bay. After yesterday's 63% Rays pick failed, the model is actually *lowering* its confidence on Tampa Bay tomorrow, which speaks to proper Bayesian updating of our priors.

This isn't revenge betting. This is following the data to a similar conclusion with adjusted expectations. The 10-point confidence drop from 63% to 53% reflects real information incorporation from yesterday's outcome.

## The Bottom Line

Yesterday: 0-2, brutal efficiency. Tomorrow: One pick at 53%, modest confidence, same team that let us down 24 hours ago. This is where discipline meets data. We don't chase losses, we follow probability matrices. See you after first pitch.

*— Stan*
